speechtext:
If hon. members want a perfect example of that kind of humour in one of Canada's great statesmen they will find it in the senator from Brockville, who has made some of the brightest remarks which have ever appeared in the Canadian press. Yet I venture to suggest that not once in all his many years has he hurt anybody in the remarks he has made.
I have just one suggestion to make. I should like to see the form and spirit of debate changed to the point where we should conceive of debate simply as a search for truth. If we were carrying on debate with that in mind, and I should happen to make a statement which causes someone to rise and to correct me, and if in doing so he has the proof that he is right and can show that I am wrong, I am not losing in the debate because I am coming nearer the truth.
And so I should like to see the practice in the house change to that extent. I should like to see debate carried on not for the purpose of beating down someone on the opposing side, or attempting to put something over them by sharp remarks. I want to see debate aim at nothing but the search for truth. When we are on a search for truth we shall get our reward, not only from our own side in politics but from the other side as well.

Upon one occasion in the house I discussed the agricultural situation. Following my remarks I went over and discussed it with the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Semi). Why should I not do that? He is a farmer who has had more experience in practical agriculture than I have had. I want to cover everything I possibly can which will help me in presenting my arguments, in the hope that through our combined efforts we may do something to improve conditions throughout the country.
I think it was Montaigne who said, when accused of plagiarism, " I gather the flowers by the wayside, by the brooks and in the meadows, and only the string with which I bind them together is my own." If every hon. member can contribute some little argument or some small effort or thought, and if by our combined efforts we can gather them together into one bouquet, then perhaps we shall have something which will help us in solving the problems of the dominion.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to compliment the mover of the resolution upon affording this opportunity of discussion. Hon. members have indicated that they want to improve the methods of functioning of the House of Commons. There seems to be agreement, too, on the point that we should spend less time in verbose discussion. I have been in the house a number of years, and I say that it is unfair time and time again to spread throughout the country the fact that it costs so much per day or so much per column of Hansard, in an effort to try to make people believe that it is all wasted money. There is more than the expenditure necessary for the mechanical running of parliament; there is a human side which must be considered. Employment is given to quite a number of people who have no employment between sessions. I see some hon. members on the other side smiling at that, but I think that is something which should be considered. I do not think I have taken more than my share of the time of this house in speaking, and I make no excuse for what I have said in the past or what I am saying at the present time.
We are 245 members duly elected by the electors of the country. We all have our own problems which taken together become national in scope. This is the only way in which we can discuss these problems. I remember quite vividly when I sat in the far comer of the house nearly twelve years ago. For the first few days I was puzzled as to why there should be so many members. To me the machinery of parliament seemed

Rules oj the House
to be top heavy and very slow moving. But after listening religiously for months to the speeches made, without making a single one myself, I began to hear the voice of British Columbia, the voices of the maritime provinces, of central Canada and of the three western provinces; I began to hear the national voice of Canada. If we took the time we should to discuss the regional and national and international questions that we should, we would be here for fourteen months in the year. I do not believe we waste any time in conducting the business of the house. Again I repeat that we should not forget that employment is given to many people who will be out of employment immediately parliament prorogues.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) has suggested that we should sit until seven o'clock. I am in favour of anything that will shorten the length of the session without decreasing the amount of work done. Every member, no matter from where he comes, is entitled to express his opinion upon any subject. It will be remembered that last year we had an exceptionally short session. That was not very pleasant for the so-called back benchers. We were told time and again that if it was not possible to prorogue parliament before the coronation, we would have to come back in the middle of the summer or early in the fall. Regardless of what legislation is introduced at this session, I believe it will be much longer because of one reason. Our constituents expect us not only to work in the committees but to express our sentiments in the house on some of the problems which the country has to face.
I believe that this resolution should be sent to a committee to be studied. I listened most attentively to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North when he suggested that the estimates should be considered by a special committee. I am absolutely against the setting up of such a committee, unless it is composed of all the members of the house. Of necessity the committee would have to be limited in number, perhaps to not more than twenty-four members. Does the hon. member expect that other members who are not on the committee will be satisfied with the reports brought in? Any hon. member would have the right to discuss each item regardless of how much time had been spent in the committee and every member of this house would have the right to scrutinize every one of these items.
I remember when it was suggested eleven years ago that speeches should be limited to forty minutes. Some members thought that would not work out; but taking myself as an
example, I believe that if I were allowed to speak only twenty minutes instead of forty, my speeches would be much better than they are at the present time. Perhaps the same thing could be said of many other hon. members. An attempt to save time is not a good thing as far as this parliament is concerned. It should not be an end but a way to good legislation. Each one of us has certain responsibilities, not only towards this parliament but towards our constituents. It is our duty to see that the questions which are dealt with are dealt with properly regardless of time.
I do not know if I am in order, but there is one matter I should like to mention. I have never liked the idea of having to take an oath to get my indemnity cheque. I submit I have a right to that regardless of how many days I have been absent from the House of Commons but I must state that I have lost very little time, however. In my time I have paid several payrolls and I have never had one of my men put his hand on the bible to swear that he had worked so many days. I believe that is my responsibility to my constituents. If they do not believe I am fulfilling my duties; if they do not think I have been in the house enough, then it is up to them to penalize me the next time I ask them for their support. I believe it is degrading to ask members of parliament to go down to the office and take an oath that they have sat so many days in the House of Commons. As far as I am concerned, I have taken that oath for the last six years, and it is not my intention to do it in the future, although I have done it for the first three years.
Mention has been made of the time taken up in recording a vote. We should adopt a system similar to that used in Great Britain. I shall not say we waste half an hour, but we lose that much time in taking a vote, whereas it should be possible to take it in ten minutes. I appreciate the opportunity given to me this afternoon to make these remarks on the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Gladstone). This is a private members' day. I have no doubt that on previous occasions it has been said that the time of the house has been wasted in discussing private members' resolutions. I believe that private members' days represent one of the most important principles of democracy. Speaker after speaker has stated that the number of private members' days should be increased, and I am entirely in favour of that suggestion. The government is represented by the members of the cabinet, but the individual members also have a responsibility. There is no doubt that some great benefits to the people as a whole have
Rules oj the House

resulted from private members' resolutions. Time and time again we see it stated in the press that parliament is a great waster of public funds; that parliament is a great waster of time; but I repeat that I consider it miraculous that we are able to complete the work of parliament in the time that we do. 3 must re-state here again that here in this parliament we have 245 members duly elected by their constituents and in their mandate the electors have the implicit right to expect that their representatives will discuss diligently and if necessary extensively regional and *national questions.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have enjoyed the speeches of the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette), the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church), the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill), and the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman). I should like "to .express my approval of virtually everything that has been said by these gentlemen. As 3 am a new member representing a new movement, perhaps it may interest other hon. members to know how we in this corner feel about the rules of the house. One of the most confusing things to a new member is the "order" chorus. This chorus seems to be consistently put in operation when a new member tries to talk. He may be out of order, but we find it exceedingly difficult to know when we are in order and to present our ideas without being interrupted and interfered with and disconcerted and generally prevented from telling in a straightforward way the things we came to tell. In the light of that situation I think the observations of the hon. member for Cochrane were exceedingly pertinent and appropriate. If there is one thing that is truer than another it is this, that what seems the radical, extreme idea of one day is looked upon as the sane, solid orthodoxy of another.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: Some of them.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
True, and who knows which of the ideas considered radical to-day will be orthodox to-morrow? That is the important thing. Nearly always the ideas which look most unorthodox to one generation are regarded as manifest platitudes to another. The history of our people so abounds in cases of that kind that it is simply a platitude for me to state it.
With respect to the resolution before us, I appreciate its having been introduced because it gives us a chance to express our ideas. Without intending any offence to the hon. member who introduced it (Mr. Gladstone), my impression is that the resolution is too

vague. I felt very sympathetic with the words of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Perhaps I may be wrong, but I have the feeling, and it is abroad throughout the land, all over the west and in many parts of the east, that there is a deliberate, secret, calculated movement aiming to suppress the popular expression of opinion, and to suppress new and popular movements, the assumption being that whatsoever is new must be wrong. Consequently in a resolution of this kind I find some ground for anxiety, and just in order to remove such anxiety it would have been better I think had the member specified in the resolution, so that we could consider them, one or two reforms which he believes desirable. If we study the history of parliamentary government among British peoples, we shall find that many attacks have been made on the rights of parliament, and some of them have succeeded in a way from which we are suffering even to-day. So I think the resolution is too vague.
We should be told, for example, to whom this committee is to report and who is to take action on its proposals. Are the proposals to be presented to this house before they are drafted in a bill?
Since we have sat here, Mr. Speaker, I have peen positively astounded at the way some things are railroaded through. Last night we had a good example of the kind of thing which under our rules may be done and what an appalling thing it is that it can be done in a great democracy like Canada. Just think of this:	If one more member
had chosen to speak or the discussion had continued five minutes longer, hon. members would not have been able to express an opinion in the form of a vote on a bill that every single member of this house enthusiastically supported; the result would have been that this country would have continued to suffer from one of the most disgusting and outrageous abuses that I believe ever began to develop in a British country, and there would have been absolutely no way of our resisting it. I refer to the bill dealing with the Performing Right Society. The feeling which was made manifest here last night so enthusiastically on that bill, has prevailed for three years, during which the people have been clamouring for a change, and for three years a bill has been brought into the house to correct this abuse, but has been killed. There is a state of affairs which manifestly is not working for democracy.
If the findings of the committee which this resolution proposes should be presented to some body not reporting directly to this house, and then if the committee's recom-

Rules oj the House
mendations are put into the form of a government measure-I do not wish to imply anything against the government, but suppose that should be done-if such measure should then come into the house with the whole strength of the party machine in operation behind it, some of the liberties at least which the minor groups in the house now enjoy could be taken away from us, and we could do absolutely nothing about it. This is too bad but it is true, so far as I have been able to judge during the short time I have been in the house.
I do not wish, Mr. Speaker, to prolong my remarks. I wish to see reforms in parliament in so far as they will really reform, but as members of this house we cannot realize too fully that the liberties and happiness not only of this generation but of generations yet unborn are in our keeping. Before, therefore, we modify anything which has been discovered and perfected and handed down to us by our fathers as safe and sane we should be very, very careful. Consequently I must oppose the resolution on the ground that it is too vague-not that I am not in favour of reform, but that I wish to be very sure that there is nothing to come out of this resolution which will do us harm instead of good.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after all, I believe the rules of the house are not so bad as some people sometimes represent them to be, and the discussion in the house this afternoon rather confirms my view.
I share to a large extent the view of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Blackmore) that it would be better if some practical suggestions were made in the resolution so that the house would know what is really involved in the proposal now before us. While no man is more favourable than I am to changes, provided they are reforms and real improvements, I do not want to change something that is good to make it less good. Our rules have come down to us as the result of the working out of parliamentary institutions in Great Britain and Canada for many, many years. Indeed, one of the sections of the British North America Act says that the privileges and powers of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada shall be those enacted by the parliament of Canada, provided they do not exceed the privileges and immunities and powers of the House of Commons and the House of Lords of Great Britain.
The rules have been changed occasionally in minor respects. There have been only two full revisions of the rules. I do not agree with the hon. member who said that every time the rules have been changed it has been for the 51952-48
purpose of curtailing the rights of private members, I think, on the contrary, that the rights of private members have not been curtailed but rather extended when a revision has been made. I had the privilege of being a member of the Speaker's committee in 1927, when the last revision was made, and the main changes made at that time were the eleven o'clock adjournment rule and the forty minute rule for speeches. The hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) says that the forty minute rule has not shortened the sessions of parliament. It is possible that it has not shortened the sessions of parliament; but I think it has prolonged the life of some of us, and it has given an opportunity to more members to express their views on any subject which comes before the house. Years ago there was no limit to either the length of the speech or the length of the session.

speechtext: Or the length of the day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
Or the
length of the day. In 1913 we sat in the House of Commons for two weeks night and day, with the exception of Sunday; at twelve o'clock on Saturday night, we being all good Christians, the house adjourned to three o'clock on Monday. There we were, divided into squads to keep the fire burning; and it was this incident that showed the necessity of the rule of closure, to which I objected strenuously and of which I complained bitterly when it was imposed. But I am free to confess that in the hectic days of 1926 I myself had to move closure, and I found it was a very good instrument to use when the circumstances justified.
Let me say that I have pondered the British parliamentary rules. I have taken my political education in the British system of parliament, and I do not agree to any extent with those who praise the United States way as regards committees and other devices. Of course it is quite different; the system is not at all the same. Ministers have no seat in congress; necessarily they must appear before committees and explain the policies of the government which have to be decided afterwards by congress. But I do not believe that anybody in this country would favour a change under which our ministers would not occupy seats in parliament. As far as I am concerned I would rather not be a minister if I had to relinquish my seat in the house.
Now, with regard to private members' rights. Mention has been made of the practice in the House of Commons in England. Perhaps hon. members know that there the government is the absolute master of parliamentary proceedings, such as the length of debates, allocation of days for a certain debate, and when

Rules of the House

the vote shall be taken; so far as private members' resolutions are concerned, there is a ballot, and the members who will have the floor on the day which is fixed for discussion are those whose names come out of the basket.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: And no more than one in twenty-five ever comes out.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
So that our system is certainly not more restrictive than the one which is used in the British House of Commons.
I have been a private member twice as long as I have been a member of a government, and I do not recall that at any time I have been deprived of a chance to say something when I had something to say. My good friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North, who is one of those who complained most, might find it difficult to recall an occasion when he has been prevented from saying something in the house.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: I did not complain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: No? That is fine. Because, apart from the resolutions and the public bills, an hon. member can always speak when the house is moved into committee of supply, except on Thursdays and Fridays; he can say anything under the sun. There is the debate on the address, and there is the chance of speaking on other members' proposals and on government measures and of saying anything that would be of practicability and of use to the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: And on the budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
And, of course, in the debate on the budget. After all, the business has to be done. The government is a committee of the House of Commons; it is an executive which is supposed to represent the House of Commons in parliament in the administration of affairs, in the carrying on of public business, and it would be impossible to go on with the business of the country if there were not some rules which at least give the government the right of way on certain days. Perhaps those days are more numerous than some hon. members would like them to be, but it is essential to make such provision; otherwise the session would be never-ending. Business could not be done properly if the rules were not substantially in the form in which they are to-day.
The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) says that the work of parliament must be one of search for truth. I quite agree with him, but I think the rules as they stand have been framed for that purpose. When he referred to the niceties of debates and the

witty repartees of my right hon. friend, I may remind him that all that has been done under the rules as they are to-day.
I am grateful and I think the house is grateful to the hon. member who moved this resolution. It has been the occasion of many suggestions which will be considered, but I believe the subject is one which needs to be studied by each hon. member individually. We were not expecting this to be a session for the revision of the rules, and I may assure the house that the work of this session will be heavy. I do not see that it would be possible to have a Speaker's committee to alter the rules of the house at the present session. However, my hon. friend's resolution has certainly served a good purpose; he has gone some way towards the end he had in view, and perhaps he will not force a division on the resolution.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
As there is hardly time left to take up effectively the succeeding notice of motion on the order paper, I should like, with respect to this discussion, to express a thought which probably was barely touched upon by some hon. gentlemen who preceded me this afternoon. It has seemed to me, in the ten or eleven sessions that I have been in this house, that one respect in which our rules are defective, at least from the public standpoint, as serving the interests of democracy, if not from the standpoint of actual debate in this chamber, is that from time to time we close the session without disposing of the business which is already on the order paper. I ask seriously whether it is not a mistake in the interests of maintaining a democratic system of government and a democratic parliament, to have the session close without private bills in some instances having had an opportunity of being dealt with. The same is true of private members' resolutions. The answer to all that is obviously that the session would run on forever and never be closed. I suggest that it might be better if we had a time limit placed upon the date, after the commencement of the session, when these matters might be put on the order paper for discussion. But I think, in the interests of the country, we ought to dispose of matters which are already on the order paper.
Let me give another illustration of what I consider an evil, if I may use that word for want of a better, of the present situation. During this session I felt compelled to divide the house, and the vote took up probably half an hour. Why did I do that? For this reason. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe), rightly or wrongly, took a position which I considered in error. Under the rules

Rules oj the House
I could not discuss that notice of motion for the production of papers in the house without its going to notices of motion, and if under the rules it went to notices of motion it had little or no chance of ever being reached. It so happens-I say this with deference to hon. gentlemen who took a different view- I am thoroughly satisfied, which I suppose is not unusual, that I was right in this particular instance, and that those who voted against me on that occasion were wrong. I am satisfied that, having regard to the legal knowledge and the judicial mind of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), I could present a case to him and have him decide in my favour in view of the British precedents which I took the trouble to look up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Of course, under the rules, my hon. friend will have another opportunity on that subject.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: Possibly, but it is doubtful unless I wish to take advantage of the opportunity on going into supply some day-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: There will be another one.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: I could suggest another opportunity apart from that.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext: I think the house should seriously consider whether we ought to amend the rules so as to provide that before the close of any particular session we shall dispose of all business which is on the order paper, even if we have to limit the date after which no matter may go upon the order paper.

subtopic: PROPOSAL FOR APPOINTMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER REVISION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to dispel the fears of the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) with regard to the wording of the resolution. Referring to the Journals of the House of Commons for 1926-27, I find a similar resolution in these words:
On motion of Mr. Mackenzie King (Prince Albert), it was resolved that,-A special committee consisting of Messrs. Lemieux, Elliott, Euler, Lapointe, Marcil, Johnston (Long Lake), Kellner, Bird, Hanson, Boys, Perley (Sir George), Black (Yukon), and MacDonald (Cape Breton South), be appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the advisability of revising the rules of the house and to report to the house at the present session.
In the same Journals, I find fifty pages devoted to the report of this committee, which gave us the rules of the house as they stand to-day.
As the sponsor of the resolution I should like to express my appreciation of the many hon. members who have contributed to the discussion, which I am confident will result in profit. I am sure it has brought to the notice of members of the government many points, particularly points in which private members are interested. There is no desire on the part of private members at any time to embarrass or impede the progress of the government, and I am sure that at all times it is their wish to facilitate government in every way and to do all those things which are in the interests of the people. Under the circumstances I am quite content that the motion should be withdrawn.
Motion withdrawn.

At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, February 24, 1938
